extracted.intended_audience: writers, subject-matter experts, advocates, and communications staff who want to pitch op-eds to media outlets
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for preparing and sending email pitches to place opinion pieces (op-eds) in newspapers and online outlets, covering outlet selection, contacts, pitch/content format, subject lines, exclusivity, follow-up, tracking, and next steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pick the right outlet
rubrics_metrics.description: Are there any specific outlets that will be interested in the piece you are about to write? Media outlets are not generic. Each one has a unique style and voice and each is interested in particular types of angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor the piece to the audience and style of target outlets and to the proclivities of the op-ed editor where known. Choose outlets that reach your target audience (e.g., CNBC for business-minded readers) and have a compelling reason to care (discusses an issue important to their readers from an unrepresented perspective). If you can't identify likely outlets, consider publishing on a blog or self-publishing instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine the best point of contact
rubrics_metrics.description: Most outlets have a general email account to receive op-ed submissions (e.g. opinion@nytimes.com). Always send your piece to the general account so it reaches the correct eyeballs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Send to the general account and, if you have it, also to the editor’s direct email (especially at large outlets). Interns and assistants often screen submissions. Use curated contact lists where available (ReThink Media's top-100 list, M+R's Opinion Page Yellow Pages) to identify the best contact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craft a compelling pitch
rubrics_metrics.description: You only have a paragraph or two to convince the editor that you are offering them a compelling piece of content that they are going to want. A persuasive pitch does at least three things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pitch should (1) establish the piece’s relevance and import to the outlet’s readers — why they should care and why now; (2) establish the author’s qualifications to comment (policy expert, personal experience, etc.); and (3) provide a teaser of the main argument. Keep it short and succinct — no more than a few sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brainstorm a compelling subject line — without pushing click-bait
rubrics_metrics.description: A catchy subject line will adequately summarize your central message while at the same time conveying news relevance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarize the central message and convey news relevance; sometimes highlight the writer’s credentials or lead with a news event (examples: “Op-ed: 5-star general says Trump’s Defense pick is unfit” or “Op-ed: Why GOP Candidates Should Address Money in Politics at Next Debate”). If you can’t think of an interesting headline, the piece may lack news value. Always draft the headline you want to frame the central argument, even if the editor may change it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer the piece as an exclusive
rubrics_metrics.description: Make it clear that you are offering the commentary as an exclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not submit the same piece to multiple outlets simultaneously — that damages relationships and most major outlets will not consider work that is being submitted elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submit in the body of the email, not as an attachment
rubrics_metrics.description: There are few, if any, editors who want to receive an op-ed submission as an attachment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paste the op-ed text directly into the body of the email (below your email signature is a suggested spot). Editors are often advised against opening attachments from unknown senders for security reasons, so avoid creating extra steps for them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the editor’s job easier
rubrics_metrics.description: Four quick rules to simplify editors' processing of your submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1) Put the word count in parentheses next to the title and never exceed the word count — this shows you follow rules and reduces editing needed. 2) Provide links to the author’s bio and prior pieces so the editor can confirm credentials. 3) Provide extensive contact information (editors may call late or on weekends). 4) Whenever possible, offer a high-resolution head shot (many outlets require one).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask for a hard deadline
rubrics_metrics.description: News cycles move fast. If you give editors too much time and they decline your piece, the news hook may have passed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request a polite, specific expedited yes-or-no (example wording: “Can you let me know by Wednesday?”). Balance urgency against sounding pushy so the editor will still want to consider the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Track email opens
rubrics_metrics.description: Apps and extensions like Sidekick and Streak that track email opens and clicks are useful when pitching op-eds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use open-tracking to inform follow-ups: if unopened, consider a new subject line; if opened only once with no response, reformulate your follow-up; if opened repeatedly, a gentle nudge adding one more reason may work. Repeated opens can indicate strong interest; no opens may mean try a different outlet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t be afraid to follow up
rubrics_metrics.description: Usually the next day is best, unless circumstances require same-day publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow up especially when tracking shows the submission hasn't been opened. Use tracking signals to time and tailor the follow-up. A brief, polite reminder can ensure your submission is read.

rubrics_metrics.name: Move on and try again
rubrics_metrics.description: If your deadline has passed, it’s time to move on. If the editor hasn’t opened or responded, move on to other outlets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tell the first outlet you contacted that you needed to explore other options if you published elsewhere or submitted elsewhere after they delayed. Research new outlets, determine the best contact person, polish and update your pitch and subject line, and resubmit. Repeated poor responses suggest refining the piece or targeting different outlets.
